title: The one who arrives
theme: One with understanding, with a held mind, always pure, reaches that place from which one is not born again.

sandhi.rule: Visarga before t becomes s, P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः).
saḥ loses its ending before a consonant, P. 6.1.132 (एतत्तदोः सुलोपोऽकोरनञ्समासे हलि).
t stays before p; final m stays before a vowel.
Final t becomes d before a voiced sound, P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते); aḥ → o before a voiced consonant, P. 6.1.114 (हशि च).

samasa.meaning: one with (a held) mind; with the suffix -ka

morphology.note: The counterpart of amanaskaḥ in 1.3.7: sa- ‘with’ + manas + -ka; Śaṅkara: «युक्तमनाः».
Present middle of jan ‘be born’ (stem jāya-).

translation.literal: ‘But he who is possessed of understanding, with [a held] mind, always pure, reaches that place from which he is not born again.’
translation.readable: ‘One who has understanding, whose mind is held and who is always pure, reaches that goal, from which there is no being born again.’

anvaya: यः तु विज्ञानवान् समनस्कः सदा शुचिः भवति, सः तु तत् पदम् आप्नोति, यस्मात् भूयः न जायते ॥
syntax: The counterpart of 1.3.7. A relative clause with three predicates (vijñānavān, samanaskaḥ, śuciḥ); the main clause sa tu tat padam āpnoti; a second relative clause, yasmād bhūyo na jāyate, describes the place.

ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: the rider who has a discerning charioteer, that is, one who knows, «विज्ञानवत्सारथ्युपेतो रथी, विद्वानित्येतत्». Raṅgarāmānuja comments on 1.3.7–8 together as the outcome of controlling the senses.
Madhva’s mūla writes the words together, सदाशुचिः, which could be read ‘always impure’; the contrast with 1.3.7 shows sadā śuciḥ, as the other witnesses space it.

metre.name: anuṣṭubh
metre.note: 17 and 16 syllables: the first pāda, yas tu vijñānavān bhavati, has nine, as in 1.3.6.

beginner: This verse completes the pair. Where the previous verse described a journey that fails, this one describes a journey that arrives. A person who has understanding, who keeps the mind steady and whose life is clean reaches 'that goal' — and it is a goal from which there is no being born again. Śaṅkara explains that this is the rider who has a wise driver: in other words, a person who knows. Having reached that place, he says, one does not fall from it and is not born again into saṃsāra. The two verses together turn the chariot picture into a choice between two outcomes, and they set up the question the next verse answers: what is this goal, the end of the road?
analogy: Like a traveller who finally reaches home after a long journey: the point of the road was never to keep travelling.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: That one with understanding, a held mind and always pure reaches that place from which one is not born again.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The second kind of rider, with a discerning charioteer, the one who knows, «विज्ञानवत्सारथ्युपेतो रथी, विद्वानित्येतत्», reaches that place; having reached it he does not fall from it and is not born again in saṃsāra, «यस्मादाप्तात्पदादप्रच्युतः सन् भूयः पुनः न जायते संसारे».

commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: His comment on 1.3.7–8 is given under 1.3.7: these two verses show the outcome of controlling the senses or not, «हयत्वेन रूपितानाम् इन्द्रियाणां वशीकरणतदभावयोः प्रयोजनं दर्शयति मन्त्रद्वयेन».

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: In our source Madhva prints 1.3.3–1.3.11 without comment and then comments once, marking it ॥ १०-१२ ॥, on the deities who preside over the senses, their objects, the mind and the intellect; he does not gloss this verse.

advaita.text: The one who knows reaches the place from which there is no falling back and no rebirth, «यस्मादाप्तात्पदादप्रच्युतः सन्».

visistadvaita.text: With 1.3.7 the verse states the outcome of mastering the senses or not, «वशीकरणतदभावयोः प्रयोजनं दर्शयति मन्त्रद्वयेन»: reaching the goal, as against falling into saṃsāra.

schools.disagreement: Both read the verse as the reward of control; what the goal is they say elsewhere (1.3.9, Viṣṇu’s highest place, which Śaṅkara also names). In our source Madhva prints 1.3.3–1.3.11 without comment and then comments once, marking it ॥ १०-१२ ॥, on the deities who preside over the senses, their objects, the mind and the intellect; he does not gloss this verse.

parallels.quote: यं प्राप्य न निवर्तन्ते तद्धाम परमं मम
parallels.note: The Gītā: the highest abode, reaching which they do not return.

parallels.quote: यद्गत्वा न निवर्तन्ते तद्धाम परमं मम
parallels.note: The same phrase, of the abode the sun does not light.

contemporary.text: A journey is defined by where it ends. The verse names no shortcut: understanding, a steady mind and a clean life are the whole of the method. (A modern reflection.)

reflect.deeper: Why is the goal described by what does not happen there — no being born again?
reflect.practice: Write down one thing that would keep your ‘reins’ steady this week, and do it.

flags.note: Madhva’s mūla writes सदाशुचिः for sadā śuciḥ; the letters are the same, only the spacing differs, so it is not listed in corrections.json, but read without a break it could mean ‘always impure’.
Madhva’s bhāṣya has no comment on this mantra: he prints 1.3.3–1.3.11 without comment, then comments once on 1.3.10–11 (his mark ॥ १०-१२ ॥), and that comment is filed under those two mantras only.
